subject: Mathematics
title: Fractions and Decimals — Step by Step
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Learn fractions, decimals and percentages with clear worked examples — perfect for Grade 6 revision.

sections.heading: What is a fraction?
sections.body: A fraction shows a part of a whole. The top number is the numerator (the parts we have), the bottom number is the denominator (the total equal parts). For example, in 3/4, we have 3 parts out of 4 equal parts.

sections.heading: Equivalent fractions
sections.body: Equivalent fractions look different but have the same value. Multiply (or divide) the top and bottom by the same number. Example: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. So 1/2 of a cake is the same as 2/4 of the cake.

sections.heading: Adding and subtracting fractions
sections.body: If the denominators are the same, just add or subtract the numerators. Example: 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5. If the denominators are different, first find a common denominator. Example: 1/2 + 1/4 → 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.

sections.heading: Fractions to decimals
sections.body: To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. Example: 1/2 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Example: 3/4 = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75.

sections.heading: Percentages
sections.body: Percent means 'out of 100'. To change a fraction to a percent, first make it out of 100. 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%. To find 40% of 250: 40/100 × 250 = 100.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. Write 1/2 as a decimal. (Answer: 0.5)
2. Add 1/3 and 1/3. (Answer: 2/3)
3. What is 25% of 80? (Answer: 20)
4. Change 4/5 to a percent. (Answer: 80%)

subject: Mathematics
title: Area, Perimeter and Shapes
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Everything about triangles, rectangles, squares and circles — formulas and examples.

sections.heading: Perimeter
sections.body: Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of a shape. Add all the sides together. Example: a rectangle 8cm long and 5cm wide has perimeter 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26cm.

sections.heading: Area of a rectangle and square
sections.body: Area = length × width. A rectangle 8cm by 5cm has area 8 × 5 = 40 cm². A square has all sides equal, so area = side × side. A square of side 6cm has area 36 cm².

sections.heading: Area of a triangle
sections.body: Area = 1/2 × base × height. If a triangle has base 12cm and height 8cm, area = 1/2 × 12 × 8 = 48 cm².

sections.heading: The circle
sections.body: Diameter is the distance across the circle through the centre. Radius is half the diameter. Circumference = π × diameter (use π = 22/7 or 3.14). Area of a circle = π × radius × radius.

sections.heading: Volume of a cuboid
sections.body: Volume = length × width × height. A cuboid 15cm long, 10cm wide and 5cm high has volume 15 × 10 × 5 = 750 cm³. Volume is measured in cubic units.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. Find the perimeter of a square with side 7cm. (Answer: 28cm)
2. Area of a triangle with base 10cm and height 6cm? (Answer: 30 cm²)
3. Volume of a cuboid 4 × 3 × 2? (Answer: 24 cm³)

subject: English Language
title: English Grammar Essentials
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, plurals and tenses — the building blocks of English.

sections.heading: Nouns
sections.body: A noun is a naming word — a person, place, animal or thing. Examples: teacher, Lusaka, dog, table. Proper nouns (Lusaka, John) start with a capital letter.

sections.heading: Verbs
sections.body: A verb is a doing word — it shows an action. Examples: run, eat, play, write. In 'The boy runs', 'runs' is the verb.

sections.heading: Adjectives
sections.body: An adjective describes a noun. Examples: big, small, beautiful, fast. In 'a red ball', 'red' is the adjective.

sections.heading: Plurals
sections.body: Most nouns add -s to make plural: book → books. Nouns ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x add -es: box → boxes. Some are irregular: child → children, mouse → mice, sheep → sheep, foot → feet.

sections.heading: Tenses — past, present, future
sections.body: Present: I eat. Past: I ate. Future: I will eat. Watch for irregular verbs: go → went, see → saw, come → came.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. Give the plural of 'goose'. (Answer: geese)
2. Which word is an adjective: happy, run, table? (Answer: happy)
3. Fill the blank: Yesterday I ___ to market. (Answer: went)

subject: Science
title: Science Basics for Juniors
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Living things, plants, the human body, water and energy — core Grade 6 Science.

sections.heading: Living and non-living things
sections.body: Living things grow, breathe, feed, move, and reproduce. Examples: plants, animals, humans. Non-living things do not do these. Examples: stones, water, air.

sections.heading: Plants and photosynthesis
sections.body: Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. This process is called photosynthesis. They give out oxygen during the day.

sections.heading: The human body
sections.body: The heart pumps blood around the body. The lungs help us breathe. The brain controls everything. The stomach digests food.

sections.heading: States of matter
sections.body: Matter has three states: solid (wood, ice), liquid (water, milk), and gas (air, steam). Heating a liquid turns it to gas (evaporation). Cooling a liquid turns it to solid (freezing).

sections.heading: Water and air
sections.body: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen. We breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The water cycle is: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. Which gas do plants give off during the day? (Answer: oxygen)
2. Which organ pumps blood? (Answer: the heart)
3. What is the process of plants making food called? (Answer: photosynthesis)

subject: History
title: Zambia: History and Independence
author: JohnWeb Team
description: From Northern Rhodesia to independence in 1964 — the story of Zambia.

sections.heading: Before the British
sections.body: The area we call Zambia was home to many peoples for thousands of years. The earliest people were the Khoisan (Bushmen), who were hunter-gatherers. Later, Bantu-speaking peoples migrated in and formed kingdoms and chiefdoms.

sections.heading: David Livingstone
sections.body: David Livingstone, a Scottish missionary and explorer, arrived in the mid-1800s. In 1855 he became the first European to see the great waterfall on the Zambezi, which he named the Victoria Falls.

sections.heading: Northern Rhodesia
sections.body: In 1911 the British joined the two territories together and called it Northern Rhodesia. The main economic activity became copper mining in the Copperbelt. Zambia was a British colony until 1964.

sections.heading: The fight for independence
sections.body: Zambians formed the Northern Rhodesia African National Congress and later the United National Independence Party (UNIP) led by Kenneth Kaunda. They campaigned for freedom through talks and peaceful resistance.

sections.heading: Independence 1964
sections.body: On 24th October 1964, Northern Rhodesia became the independent Republic of Zambia. Kenneth Kaunda became the first President. The new name 'Zambia' comes from the Zambezi River.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. What was Zambia called before independence? (Answer: Northern Rhodesia)
2. In which year did Zambia become independent? (Answer: 1964)
3. Who was the first President of Zambia? (Answer: Kenneth Kaunda)

subject: Geography
title: Zambia's Geography
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Rivers, lakes, provinces, weather and the map of Zambia.

sections.heading: Where is Zambia?
sections.body: Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa. It is surrounded by eight countries: Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Namibia, Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

sections.heading: Provinces
sections.body: Zambia has ten provinces: Central, Copperbelt, Eastern, Luapula, Lusaka, Muchinga, Northern, North-Western, Southern and Western.

sections.heading: Rivers and lakes
sections.body: The Zambezi is Zambia's longest river and flows through the Victoria Falls. Other rivers include the Kafue, Luangwa and Luapula. Zambia has lakes Tanganyika, Bangweulu, Mweru and the man-made Lake Kariba.

sections.heading: Weather and seasons
sections.body: Zambia has three seasons: the cool dry season (May to August), the hot dry season (September to October), and the rainy season (November to April).

sections.heading: Direction and maps
sections.body: Maps show places and directions. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. A compass shows north, south, east and west. The Equator divides the earth into north and south.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. Which river flows through Victoria Falls? (Answer: the Zambezi)
2. How many provinces does Zambia have? (Answer: ten)
3. In which direction does the sun rise? (Answer: east)

subject: Social Studies
title: Zambia: Flag, Symbols and Culture
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Understand the Zambian flag, national symbols and our rich culture.

sections.heading: The Zambian flag
sections.body: The flag has four colours: green (for the land and natural resources), red (for the blood of our heroes), black (for the people of Zambia), and orange (for the copper and mineral wealth).

sections.heading: The eagle
sections.body: An orange African fish eagle flies above the coloured bands. The eagle represents the ability of the nation to rise above its problems.

sections.heading: The national anthem
sections.body: The Zambian national anthem is 'Stand and Sing of Zambia, Proud and Free'. It was written after independence.

sections.heading: The national bird
sections.body: The national bird of Zambia is the African fish eagle. It is also featured on the flag.

sections.heading: Culture and ceremonies
sections.body: Zambia has over 70 ethnic groups with rich traditions. Famous ceremonies include the Kuomboka of the Lozi, the Ncwala of the Ngoni, and the Kulamba of the Chewa.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. What does the green colour on the flag stand for? (Answer: the land and natural resources)
2. What is the national bird? (Answer: the African fish eagle)
3. Name one traditional ceremony. (Answer: Kuomboka / Ncwala / Kulamba)

subject: Civic Education
title: Civic Education: Rights and Responsibilities
author: JohnWeb Team
description: Democracy, voting, rights, responsibilities and national symbols.

sections.heading: What is democracy?
sections.body: Democracy means government by the people. Citizens choose their leaders by voting. Zambia is a representative democracy.

sections.heading: Rights of a citizen
sections.body: Citizens have rights including: the right to life, education, health, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly, and equality before the law.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body: With rights come responsibilities: obeying the law, paying taxes, voting, respecting others, protecting the environment, and helping the community.

sections.heading: Voting
sections.body: Voting allows citizens to choose their leaders and hold them accountable. Every eligible Zambian should register and vote in elections.

sections.heading: National symbols
sections.body: National symbols include the flag, the national anthem, the eagle, and the national seal. They represent unity, pride and the values of the nation.

sections.heading: Practice questions
sections.body:
1. What is democracy? (Answer: government by the people)
2. Name one responsibility of a citizen. (Answer: obeying the law / paying taxes / voting)
3. Who is the head of state in Zambia? (Answer: the President)
